definition: Commodious means roomy, with comfortable space to spare.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word commodious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know commodious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The old station wagon proved commodious enough to swallow four duffel bags, two dogs, and a week of groceries.
Roomy stops short of commodious — a roomy trunk merely fits everything, while a commodious cabin offers generous space to live in.
Cavernous goes further than commodious — a cavernous hangar is so vast it echoes, long past feeling comfortable.

Spacious praises a place for offering plenty of open, usable room — a spacious lobby lets a crowd move freely. Commodious adds that the space is arranged so living and working in it feel easy. Both compliment space that serves people; neither describes hugeness that has outrun all use.

Capacious means able to hold a great deal — a capacious trunk swallows whatever you load into it, and the word measures pure holding power. Commodious cares about comfort instead: a commodious cabin offers generous, well-arranged room to live in, not just storage to fill.

Commodious means roomy, with comfortable space to spare.

When the scouts pitched the surplus army tent, they found it commodious beyond their hopes: twelve sleeping bags fit in a ring, packs stacked along the canvas, and there was still headroom to stand and dress by lantern light.
Commodious is more precise than just 'big' or 'roomy' because it praises space that serves comfort—room arranged so that living in it feels easy, not merely a large number of square feet.
formal / slightly old-fashioned
Commodious is a formal, slightly old-fashioned word that flatters a space: it says the room is not just large but comfortable to live and move in.
For everyday talk, 'roomy' or 'spacious' is plainer; reach for commodious in a description meant to charm — a listing, a review, a tour.

The renovation committee argued for weeks about the old reading room, which was large but never loved.
The architect's diagnosis was blunt: the room had size without comfort -- hard chairs against the far wall, one shared table, outlets nowhere.
Her redesign added no square footage at all.
It rearranged what was there: deep chairs by the windows, lamps at every elbow, small tables spaced so no one reads over a stranger's shoulder.
Students now call the room commodious, and they mean something the old room never was: a place with space to spare for actually working in.
The head librarian's report put it simply: 'Same walls.
The room finally fits the people in it.'
